newsitem.title: UK: Experts meet in London to save tiger.
newsitem.headline: Experts meet in London to save tiger.

text.p: Tiger experts from around the world met at London Zoo on Wednesday for the first major convention on tiger conservation for 10 years.

With tiger numbers dwindling, pressure is mounting for conservationists to step up the fight to save Indian, Amur, Indochinese and Sumatran tigers from extinction, according to the Zoological Society of London (ZSL).

"We are holding the symposium now because the situation is desperate," said Richard Burge, ZSL director general. "The aim is to bring together the most up to date information so conservationists can assess the problem."
Three of the eight subspecies of tigers have already become extinct this century, and the survival of those remaining is threatened by poaching and degradation of their habitat.
The 11-year old male tiger pacing around a muddy enclosure at London Zoo is one of only 650 Sumatran tigers left in the world -- only 400 of them being in the wild.

They are being pushed into small, isolated reserves by the growing human population in Sumatra, so that inbreeding is becoming as much a problem as poaching. The Indian tiger population is estimated at just 2,500.
Tigers fetch a high price on the black market as parts of their body including bones, the brain, the penis and even the eyeballs are used in traditional Asian medicine.

Delegates at the conference will hear about projects currently under way such as a breeding centre set up in Java, Indonesia in 1992. They will also hear the results of the 1995 Way Kambas project in Sumatra which used camera traps to monitor tigers over a 15-month period.
But scientists at the Tigers 2000 Symposium, which is sponsored by oil giant Esso, said it was important to step up action while there was still a chance to save the species.
"The crisis has come upon us in the last 10 years," said Burge, "but it has not yet reached a point where the tiger is committed to extinction."

If tiger numbers do drop below crucial levels, the conservationists said they would have to consider emergency procedures such as artificial insemination of females in the wild with sperm from captive males.
